question: What is the nominal voltage of the DA 40 D's electrical system?

options.text: 12 Volt DC
14 Volt DC
24 Volt DC
28 Volt DC

explanation: The DA 40 D has a 12 Volt DC electrical system, sub-divided into power generation, storage, distribution and consumers.

question: What is the rated output of the alternator, and where is it mounted?

options.text: 120 ampere, on the bottom left side of the engine, driven by a flat-belt
90 ampere, on the bottom left side of the engine, driven by a flat-belt
60 ampere, on the bottom right side of the engine, driven by a flat-belt
90 ampere, on the top of the engine, gear-driven

explanation: Power generation comes from a 90 ampere alternator mounted on the bottom left side of the engine and driven by a flat-belt.

question: What protects the alternator's power output line where it connects to the battery bus?

options.text: A 30 A circuit breaker on the instrument panel
A 5 A fuse behind the instrument panel
A 100 A fuse in the relay junction box
A 50 A fuse in the relay junction box

explanation: The alternator's output line connects to the battery bus through a 100 A fuse in the relay junction box on the firewall's left-hand side.

question: In the event of a main battery failure, what energizes the alternator field to keep it producing power?

options.text: The ECU backup battery under the rear right seat
A capacitor bank in the relay junction box
The hot battery bus, via the accessory power socket
A 12 V, 1.3 Ah sealed-lead-acid 'excitation' battery behind the instrument panel

explanation: A small 12 V, 1.3 Ah sealed-lead-acid 'excitation' battery behind the instrument panel energizes the alternator field if the main battery fails, connected via the ENGINE MASTER switch through a 5 A fuse.

question: What voltage range does the alternator's voltage regulator hold the output voltage within?

options.text: Between 12 and 14 V
Between 11 and 13 V
Between 13 and 15 V
Between 12.6 and 15.5 V

explanation: The alternator's voltage regulator (internal or external, depending on part number) regulates output voltage between 12 and 14 V.

question: What is the capacity and chemistry of the 'main' battery that stores power for the DA 40 D?

options.text: 24 V, 23 Ah lead-acid, mounted on the left-hand side of the firewall
12 V, 23 Ah lead-acid, mounted on the right-hand side of the firewall
12 V, 12 Ah sealed-lead-acid, mounted under the rear right seat
12 V, 1.3 Ah sealed-lead-acid, mounted behind the instrument panel

explanation: The 'main' battery is a 12 V, 23 Ah lead-acid battery on the firewall's right-hand side, distinct from the smaller excitation and ECU backup batteries.

question: What is the purpose of the 12 V, 12 Ah sealed-lead-acid 'ECU backup' battery under the rear right seat?

options.text: It supplies the starter motor if the main battery is depleted
It powers the avionics bus if the alternator fails
It is a further power source for the Engine Control Unit, for ECU B only
It powers the flood light and attitude gyro for one hour in the IFR model

explanation: The ECU backup battery exists purely as a further source of power for the ECU, and only for ECU B - it is automatically connected via a 30 A fuse if the alternator fails and the main battery is depleted.

question: In the IFR model, when the EMERGENCY switch is set to ON, for how long does the non-rechargeable emergency battery supply the attitude gyro and flood light?

options.text: 30 minutes
2 hours
45 minutes
1 hour

explanation: Setting the EMERGENCY switch to ON supplies the attitude gyro and flood light from the non-rechargeable dry battery for 1 hour, independent of all other consumers.

question: How often must the IFR model's non-rechargeable emergency battery cells be replaced?

options.text: Every 2 years, or after use (broken seal on the switch)
Every year, regardless of use
Every 100 hours, regardless of use
Only when the ECU BACKUP UNSAFE light illuminates

explanation: The emergency battery cells are replaced every 2 years or after use, indicated by a broken seal on the EMERGENCY switch; it is also checked at each 100 hour inspection.

question: Which bus is directly connected to the main battery via a 50 A fuse and cannot be disconnected from it?

options.text: The ECU bus
The hot battery bus
The essential bus
The main bus

explanation: The hot battery bus is permanently, directly connected to the main battery through a 50 A fuse and powers the map/reading light and accessory power plug.

question: Which switch controls the 'battery' relay that connects the main battery to the battery bus?

options.text: The AVIONIC MASTER switch
The ESSENTIAL BUS switch
The ELECTRIC MASTER key switch
The ENGINE MASTER switch

explanation: The 'battery' relay, which connects the main battery to the battery bus, is controlled by the ELECTRIC MASTER key switch.

question: Which switch must be ON to connect the ECU A and ECU B to the ECU bus?

options.text: The ELECTRIC MASTER switch
The AVIONIC MASTER switch
The ESSENTIAL BUS switch
The ENGINE MASTER switch

explanation: The ECU bus is directly connected to the battery bus and provides power to ECU A and ECU B only when the ENGINE MASTER switch is set to ON.

question: In the event of an alternator failure, what does switching ON the ESSENTIAL BUS switch achieve?

options.text: It separates the main bus from the battery bus and essential bus, tying the essential bus to the hot battery bus instead
It disconnects the ECU bus entirely, stopping the engine
It shuts off all avionics immediately
It reconnects the alternator field automatically

explanation: Switching the ESSENTIAL BUS switch ON separates the main bus, and ties the essential bus to the hot battery bus, providing limited-time battery power to the equipment essential for safe flight and landing.

question: What voltage does the voltmeter actually display under normal operating conditions?

options.text: The hot battery bus voltage at all times
The alternator voltage, since it shows the ECU bus voltage
The excitation battery voltage only
The average of the main and ECU backup battery voltages

explanation: The voltmeter shows the voltage of the ECU bus, which under normal conditions is the alternator voltage; if the alternator is offline, it shows whichever battery is then connected to the ECU bus.

question: After how many minutes of engine operation should the voltmeter indication normally be in the green range?

options.text: After 20 minutes
After 5 minutes
After 10 minutes
After 2 minutes

explanation: Before the alternator reaches operating temperature the voltage indication may sit in the upper yellow range; after 10 minutes of engine operation it should be in the green range.

question: On a conventional instrument panel, after how long in the yellow voltage range does the ENGINE caution light illuminate?

options.text: Longer than 5 minutes
Longer than 30 seconds
Longer than 10 minutes
Longer than 1 minute

explanation: If the voltage indication stays in the yellow range for longer than 1 minute, the ENGINE caution light illuminates on a conventional instrument panel.

question: What does the ammeter display?

options.text: The intensity of current supplied to the electrical system by the alternator
The current drawn by the starter motor only
The state of charge of the main battery as a percentage
The current flowing through the ECU backup battery only

explanation: The ammeter shows the current the alternator is supplying to the electrical system, including the current used to charge the battery.

question: What secondary protection, beyond the thermal switch, is built into the Pitot heating system?

options.text: An automatic switch to the alternate static source
A thermal fuse, which if activated stops the Pitot heat being switched on and requires servicing
A second, backup Pitot probe with independent heating
A manual circuit breaker only, with no thermal protection

explanation: Beyond the thermal switch that keeps temperature constant, a thermal fuse provides additional protection; once it activates, Pitot heating cannot be switched on again and the system needs servicing.

question: What happens automatically after the ELECTRIC MASTER is switched to ON, as part of the pre-flight check of the annunciator panel?

options.text: Only the WARNING light flashes; caution and status lights remain off
The aural alert sounds continuously until the acknowledge button is pressed
A functional check starts automatically: all lights flash and the aural alert is muted
All lights immediately extinguish to show a clean test

explanation: Switching ELECTRIC MASTER to ON automatically starts a functional check: all annunciator lights flash while the aural alert is muted, until the acknowledge button is pressed.

question: How does a pilot initiate the additional annunciator panel system test, beyond the automatic power-up check?

options.text: By pressing the ECU TEST button twice in quick succession
By cycling the ELECTRIC MASTER OFF then ON three times
By holding the acknowledge button for 5 seconds
By holding the acknowledge button for 2 seconds

explanation: Holding the acknowledge button for 2 seconds starts an additional system test, in which all lights blink and the aural alert sounds continuously.

question: How is a Warning message on the annunciator panel indicated before the acknowledge button is pressed?

options.text: A continuous aural alert, a blinking red WARNING light, and a blinking red light for the affected system
A momentary aural alert and a solid amber CAUTION light only
A blinking white status light with no aural alert
A single aural chime with no light indication

explanation: A warning is indicated by a continuous aural alert plus the blinking red WARNING light and the affected system's own blinking red light, until acknowledged.

question: After the acknowledge button is pressed for an active warning, what happens to the affected system's red light?

options.text: It starts flashing faster
It changes from blinking to solid illumination
It extinguishes completely
It begins blinking amber instead of red

explanation: Pressing acknowledge stops the aural alert and extinguishes the WARNING light, but the affected system's own warning light changes from blinking to a solid illumination rather than going out.

question: What specifically triggers the START warning light?

options.text: The starter has been operated for more than 10 seconds continuously
The ELECTRIC MASTER key is left in the START position for over 2 minutes
The starter motor's pinion has not disengaged from the engine after starting
The battery voltage drops below 11 V during cranking

explanation: The START warning is displayed when the connection between the starter motor and the engine has not been broken - the starter pinion remaining engaged.

question: While the starter is actually being operated, does the START light illuminating also trigger the WARNING light and aural alert?

options.text: Yes - both are triggered every time the starter is used
Only the aural alert is triggered, not the WARNING light
Only the WARNING light is triggered, not the aural alert
No - the START light illuminates continuously during normal starter operation without the WARNING light or aural alert

explanation: The START light is continuously illuminated for as long as the starter is being operated, which is normal - in that case the WARNING light and aural alert are not activated.

question: What terminates the low voltage caution message once it has been triggered below 12.6 volts?

options.text: The voltage exceeding 12.9 volts again
The voltage exceeding 12.6 volts again
Pressing the acknowledge button, regardless of voltage
Switching to ECU B

explanation: The low voltage caution activates below 12.6 V and is only terminated once the voltage recovers above 12.9 V - not immediately at 12.6 V again.

question: What do the two white status lights, FUEL TRANS and GLOW, indicate?

options.text: FUEL TRANS: a fuel leak has been detected; GLOW: the starter is engaged
FUEL TRANS: the transfer pump is active; GLOW: the glow plugs are active
FUEL TRANS: low fuel in the main tank; GLOW: the ECU is in test mode
FUEL TRANS: the emergency fuel valve is in EMERG. TRANSFER; GLOW: high oil temperature

explanation: FUEL TRANS is illuminated only while the electric transfer pump is actually running; GLOW is illuminated only while the glow plugs are active.
